title: ACP session options and resource telemetry UX
description:
## Problem Statement

LouiseLM can select an adapter only when the first chat is created, and it currently discards ACP session configuration options and usage/context updates. Users cannot change an agent-advertised model or reasoning setting after startup, cannot see which settings are active, and cannot tell whether a long autonomous session is approaching its context limit or waiting on a permission request. Starting multiple sessions also lacks explicit navigation and cleanup controls.

## Solution

Add a generic ACP session-controls and observability UX. After `session/new` becomes ready, open a token-free setup overview of all supported agent-advertised select and boolean options; allow idle-only changes through a public chat method and `:LouiselmSessionOptions`, refreshing the complete option list after each update. Add explicit `:LouiselmCancel`, `:LouiselmNewSession`, `:LouiselmSwitchSession`, and `:LouiselmCloseSession` commands. Keep existing sessions running when a new one starts, expose their state through compact headers and switcher rows, and dispose sessions explicitly when closed. Render passive context-pressure states, reported cumulative cost, active settings, lifecycle state, permission waiting, compaction/tool activity, and optional experimental per-turn usage fields without estimating tokens or prices.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I want to choose model and other ACP session options before my first prompt, so that each new session starts with deliberate settings.
2. As a user, I want to change supported options while a session is idle, so that future turns use the new configuration without restarting the session.
3. As a user, I want busy sessions to refuse option changes and offer explicit cancellation, so that autonomous turns are not reconfigured mid-flight.
4. As a user, I want to see active settings, lifecycle state, context pressure, cost, and reported usage, so that I can monitor long-running work.
5. As a user, I want to create, switch between, and close concurrent sessions, so that multiple adapters can work without leaking processes.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A ready new session with supported ACP config options opens an overview picker before the first prompt; Esc accepts agent defaults and an agent with no supported options skips the picker.
2. The overview renders every supported select/boolean option in agent order, supports selecting values, applies `session/set_config_option`, replaces the local list with the complete response, and handles agent-pushed `config_option_update` notifications.
3. Option changes are rejected while prompting, cancelling, or waiting for permission; `:LouiselmCancel` requests cancellation and late callbacks cannot revive disposed UI or sessions.
4. The client advertises boolean config-option support and ignores unknown future option types while rejecting malformed consumed fields.
5. `:LouiselmNewSession` chooses an adapter, creates a separate session, and opens its setup picker without cancelling existing sessions; `:LouiselmSwitchSession` selects attached sessions using compact agent/state/options/context/cost rows.
6. `:LouiselmCloseSession` confirms only for active or permission-blocked sessions, disposes the selected session/process, removes its chat buffer, and leaves other sessions running.
7. Session headers show exact lifecycle/activity state, all active options, context used/size/percentage with passive 75/90/95% warning states, stale context after model changes until refreshed, and reported cumulative cost when available.
8. Completed turns append a compact usage footer only for reported fields; optional experimental usage fields are validated defensively, never estimated or supplemented with adapter-specific fallbacks.
9. Compaction remains agent-owned: render generic ACP tool/compaction activity and context-meter changes, but add no LouiseLM manual compaction API in this phase.
10. Headless session snapshots/events expose typed configuration, lifecycle, permission, context, cost, and usage state for a future monitor; no swarm dashboard or orchestration is included.

## Implementation Notes

- Extend the session lifecycle and ACP validation at the shared boundary; preserve complete option-list replacement and asynchronous main-loop scheduling.
- Enrich `session:inspect()` and typed events rather than deriving telemetry from rendered buffers.
- Keep `LLM_MODEL` in the caller-owned schema/config example; do not add a universal built-in schema that rejects provider-specific environment variables.
- Preserve agent-provided defaults, session history, cumulative cost, and existing slash-command passthrough. Mark context telemetry stale after model changes until the agent reports a new effective window.

## Testing Notes

- Add focused mini.test coverage for option parsing, dependent option refresh, boolean capability advertisement, malformed/unknown options, idle-only transitions, cancellation, permission waiting, and disposal/late results.
- Add headless UI smoke tests for setup/overview flow, command behavior, headers, passive thresholds, usage footer omission, compaction/tool rendering, multiple-session navigation, and close confirmation.
- Exercise ACP notifications and process callbacks through scheduled production boundaries; use the mock ACP agent and no real credentials or agent binaries.

## Out of Scope

- Manual compaction or a hard-coded `:LouiselmCompact` command.
- A generic advertised-command picker.
- A swarm dashboard, orchestration, capacity policy, worktree isolation, or subagent aggregation.
- Adapter-specific usage parsers, pricing tables, tokenizers, or cache-cost estimates.
- A universal built-in configuration schema.
close_reason: Implemented ACP select/boolean session options, typed lifecycle/context/cost/usage state, setup and multi-session commands, safe scheduled UI updates, documentation, and passing StyLua/LuaLS/95-test gates

title: Claude file edits are auto-denied because the ACP diff content is ignored
description:
Every file edit requested by claude-agent-acp is refused without a review ever opening.

## Observed (session claude/0503f972-01db-4158-ac62-e89cce3de188, 2026-08-17)

~/.local/state/acp-llm-adapter/20260817-063214-181953-claude-agent-acp-stdout-jsonrpc.log line 36:

  PERMISSION id=2 kind=edit "Edit qa-diff-test.txt"
    rawInput keys: [file_path, old_string, new_string, replace_all]
    content: [{"type":"diff","path":"/home/lotso/code/louiselm/qa-diff-test.txt","oldText":"hello","newText":"hello world"}]

line 37: tool_call_update failed, rawOutput "Tool permission request failed: Error: Tool use aborted".

## Root cause

lua/louiselm/ui/diff/init.lua:29 request_edit reads the edit payload only from toolCall.rawInput, looking for diff / content / newText / new_text. Claude sends the Edit tool arguments verbatim there (file_path, old_string, new_string, replace_all) and puts the reviewable text in toolCall.content as an ACP diff entry, which louiselm never reads. So Apply.normalize fails with "diff edit must contain diff or content", Diff:open returns false, and lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua writes an error line then cancels the request. The cancelled outcome is what the agent reports as "Tool use aborted".

Net effect: the diff review has never worked with this agent, and every edit is silently denied.

## Fix direction

- Read the first toolCall.content entry of type "diff". When it carries oldText, the payload is an exact-text replacement of a fragment, not whole-file content; when it does not, newText is the whole file.
- Teach louiselm.ui.diff.apply a replacement form alongside diff and content so the preview shows the real before/after.
- Keep the rawInput path working for agents that populate it.

## Acceptance

- A request shaped like the payload above opens a review showing -hello / +hello world, and accepting sends the allow option.
- A replacement whose old text is not in the file fails with an actionable error instead of a silent cancel.
- replace_all is honored: false replaces the first occurrence only.
close_reason: Fixed in a57cee2 (diff UI now falls back to the ACP diff content entry when rawInput lacks diff/content). Verified live by the permissions QA round (QA_REVIEW-permissions-round.md, now archived as louiselm-aib): case 6 (F1 regression, gates cases 3-5) passed — review buffer opened, 'a' applied the edit, file read back 'hello world'. Bead was never closed despite the fix landing and being verified; closed now while retroactively archiving that round.

title: LouiselmToMarkdown: export session transcript from structured JSONL
description:
## Goal
A LouiselmToMarkdown user command that exports a louiselm session's full transcript to a markdown file, reconstructed from the session's structured JSONL data — not a scrape of the rendered chat buffer.

## Scope
- In scope: new command registered alongside the existing Louiselm* commands (LouiselmResume, LouiselmSessionId, etc.) in the chat command module; reads from the same session/transcript data those commands already access; writes full tool commands and full tool results/output (not one-line summaries or truncated text); takes a session id (defaults to current session if omitted).
- Out of scope: any blog-specific behavior (scaffolding, literalinclude stubbing) — this command only exports one session to one markdown file and knows nothing about blog/.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. Given a session id, running the command produces a markdown file containing the full reconstructed transcript: every user message, every assistant message, every tool call with its full command and full result/output.
2. Given no session id, the command operates on the current session.
3. Output is deterministic for a given session (same input transcript produces the same markdown, modulo an output path/timestamp).
4. Existing manually-copied transcripts (e.g. the buffer-scrape currently at the louiselm repo root) are visibly less complete than this command's output — spot-check against one real session confirms previously-truncated tool output is now present in full.

## Testing
- Unit test against a fixture session JSONL asserting full tool commands/results appear in the output, not truncated summaries.
- Existing session/transcript module test patterns apply; no new UI/buffer testing needed.

## Notes
- This is real, discoverable plugin surface (unlike the rest of the parent feature's blog/ tooling) — it is useful to any louiselm user independent of blogging.
- Parent feature: louiselm-r1k.
close_reason: LouiselmToMarkdown command implemented and tested: registered in lua/louiselm/ui/chat/command.lua, Chat:to_markdown in lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua, rendering via louiselm.session.transcript. Full tool commands/output (untruncated), defaults to current session, deterministic output, dedicated test coverage in tests/ui/chat_to_markdown_spec.lua (8/8 passing) plus tests/session/transcript_export_spec.lua. Shipped across commits 4e4a58b, 6167df0, 14dbab6.

title: myst build --html fails with ECONNREFUSED to its own localhost:3000 prerender server under Docker bridge networking
description:
`myst build --html --strict` (the exact command the new `.gitlab-ci.yml` pages job runs, on the exact `node:24-bookworm` image it pins) fails deterministically inside a plain `docker run` container using Docker's default bridge network, but succeeds on a bare host and succeeds inside the same container under `--network host`. This is an open risk for the real GitLab CI pipeline (louiselm-zce), unconfirmed because this sandbox has no live GitLab Runner to test against.

## Observed

Session: CI setup work for louiselm-zce (GitLab CI build+deploy of blog/ to GitLab Pages), 2026-08-18, in /home/lotso/code/louiselm sandbox with Docker 29.6.2 (overlayfs, cgroup v2, kernel 7.0.13+deb13-amd64).

Three reproductions of the identical command sequence `npm install -g mystmd@1.10.1 && cd blog && myst build --html --strict`:

1. Bare host, asdf-managed Node v24.16.0, no container: exit 0, `blog/_build/html/index.html` produced with real content. Ran twice, succeeded both times.
2. `docker run --rm -v <repo>:/repo -w /repo --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" node:24-bookworm bash -c '...'` with Docker's default bridge network (`docker network inspect bridge` shows `"EnableIPv6": false`, subnet `172.17.0.0/16`): exit 1, 3/3 runs. Build log (identical each time):
   ```
   🔌 Server started on port 3000!  🥳 🎉
   	👉  http://localhost:3000  👈
   Fetch of http://localhost:3000 threw an error (Attempt #1) FetchError: request to http://localhost:3000/ failed, reason: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:3000
   ... (repeats for /post-example/blog, /index.json, /post-example.blog.json, /robots.txt)
   Fetch of http://localhost:3000 threw an error (Attempt #2) ...
   Fetch of http://localhost:3000 threw an error (Attempt #3) ...
   Failed to fetch http://localhost:3000 after 3 attempts.
   Myst CLI Versions:
    - node                        24.19.0     Required: >= 18.0.0
    - npm                         11.17.0     Required: >=8.6.0
    - myst                         1.10.1
   ```
3. Same container/command but `docker run --network host ...`: exit 0, 1/1 run, full successful build log with `GET / 200`, `GET /post-example/blog 200`, etc.

Root cause is unknown — not simple loopback breakage: a minimal manual repro in the same bridge-mode container (`node -e "http.createServer(...).listen(4000, () => fetch('http://localhost:4000/'))"`) succeeded fine, both with default `::` bind and explicit `127.0.0.1` bind. So the failure is specific to mystmd's book-theme dev-server startup path under bridge networking, not a blanket "loopback fetch doesn't work" issue.

## Symptoms

- What a CI job running this exact command inside a Docker-executor container with default (bridge) networking might see: the `myst build --html --strict` step fails with exit 1 and the pipeline job goes red, even though nothing about the blog content is broken.
- Error text: `FetchError: request to http://localhost:3000/ failed, reason: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:3000`, followed by `Failed to fetch http://localhost:3000 after 3 attempts.`

## Root cause

Unknown. Hypotheses, not yet discriminated:

1. Docker bridge-mode NAT/userland-proxy hairpin latency delays the container's own published port becoming reachable via `localhost`, and mystmd's book-theme prerender step's 3 retries (short interval, not measured) aren't enough margin under that added latency — would be a timing/robustness gap in mystmd's book-theme server startup (fixed asynchronously logs "started" possibly before actually ready to accept), not a hard capability gap.
2. Something specific to this sandboxed/nested-Docker environment's bridge network implementation (this sandbox is itself a constrained/virtualized environment) that would NOT reproduce on a normal cloud VM running a normal GitLab Docker-executor runner.

Nothing in this investigation distinguishes between these two. A real GitLab Runner is required to know which applies.

## Why it was not caught

There is no automated CI yet (this bug was found while building the very first `.gitlab-ci.yml` for this repo) and no live GitLab Runner reachable from this sandbox, so the only verification possible was local reproduction of the exact command/image, which surfaced this discrepancy but can't confirm whether it will recur on the real runner.

## Fix direction

Do not speculatively patch `.gitlab-ci.yml` for this (e.g. forcing host networking isn't controllable from `.gitlab-ci.yml` — it's a GitLab Runner `config.toml` `[runners.docker] network_mode` setting, out of this repo's control). Instead:

1. Watch the first real pipeline run of the `pages` job (in `.gitlab-ci.yml`, already carries an inline comment flagging this) for the exact `ECONNREFUSED ... :3000` signature during the `myst build` step.
2. If it recurs on the real runner: escalate to whoever administers the GitLab Runner to check/change the Docker executor's `network_mode`, or file upstream against `jupyter-book/mystmd` (book-theme prerender retry/backoff robustness).
3. If it does NOT recur: close this as sandbox-environment-specific and not a real risk.

## Acceptance

- A real GitLab CI pipeline run of the `pages` job in `.gitlab-ci.yml` either succeeds (closes this as sandbox-specific noise) or reproduces the same `ECONNREFUSED :3000` signature (confirms the risk and triggers the escalation above).

## Not covered

- Whether GitLab.com shared runners vs. this project's actual self-hosted `gitlab.bartab.fr` runner(s) would behave differently — runner topology for `gitlab.bartab.fr` is unknown from this sandbox.
- Whether pinning a different Node major (e.g. `node:20-bookworm`, `node:22-bookworm`) avoids the issue — not tested; the discrepancy was isolated to bridge-vs-host Docker networking, not Node version, so this seems unlikely to matter but wasn't ruled out.

title: Chat UI buffer updates run in fast event context
description: Running :LouiselmChat and receiving ACP process output raises E5560 because lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua calls nvim_buf_is_valid and other buffer APIs directly from the fast-event stdout callback. Marshal session event handling to the main loop while preserving event order and ignoring disposed views.

title: Add work-tracking section to AGENTS.md and add CLAUDE.md pointer
description:
Add the work-tracking conventions to `AGENTS.md` and make it the loaded entrypoint for every adapter.

`AGENTS.md` is currently 214 lines across 11 sections and never mentions beads, so an agent entering the repo cold cannot learn that beads is the task graph. It is also not auto-loaded by Claude Code, which reads a root `CLAUDE.md` that does not exist here.

## What to do

Insert a new **section 2**, immediately after Project Scope, and renumber the existing sections 2-11 to 3-12. Reading order should be *what this project is* → *how work is found and tracked* → *how code must be written*.

Write it by hand in the file's existing register: terse, imperative, opinionated. Around 15 lines. It must state:

- beads is the task graph for this project; `.beads/` is tracked in git
- file findings as beads before fixing them, including work deliberately deferred
- use `br` and `bv` rather than reading `.beads/*.jsonl` directly
- prefer draining in-progress work before starting new work, even when `bv` scores an unstarted item higher
- never run bare `bv` (it opens a blocking TUI); use the `--robot-*` flags

Point at `br robot-docs` for command syntax instead of duplicating a cheatsheet.

Add one line linking the example workflow document (from the sibling task) and stating plainly that it is **not binding**.

Then add a root `CLAUDE.md` containing only a pointer to `AGENTS.md`. It must stay a pointer — instruction content in both files guarantees silent drift.

## Do not use `br agents --add`

It emits roughly 60 lines of generic beads tutorial inside a `<!-- br-agent-instructions-v1 -->` block. The register clashes with `AGENTS.md`; it teaches syntax already available from `br --help` while saying nothing about this project's conventions; and `br agents --update` overwrites that block, so hand-written conventions placed inside it are destroyed on the next update.

## Acceptance criteria

- `AGENTS.md` has a work-tracking section at position 2, in the file's own voice, and later sections are renumbered consistently with no duplicate or skipped numbers.
- The section references `br robot-docs` rather than inlining command syntax.
- The link to the example workflow document states it is non-binding.
- Root `CLAUDE.md` exists and contains a pointer only, with no instruction content of its own.
- No `<!-- br-agent-instructions-v1 -->` block is present.
close_reason: AGENTS.md section 2 added (sections renumbered 3-12), CLAUDE.md pointer added, docs/example-workflow.md written, triage requirement commented onto qbr.3/qbr.5, all seven memory notes migrated to repo or user-level instructions

title: QA round: permission decision handling
description:
# Manual QA review — permission decision handling

Working file for the current QA round. You run the steps, I edit this file as we
learn. Untracked on purpose; tell me to commit or delete it when we are done.

**Round complete — all six cases passed.** Build verified: `c639f95`, `0ed18d0`,
`b76a95d` (permission serialization, cross-session decision queue, command picker
refusal), plus the three fixes this round found: `a57cee2` (F1), `348c6fc` (F3),
`c0ae0aa` (F4).

Origin: `louiselm-4wx` — two parallel tool calls produced two overlapping
`session/request_permission` requests, one was answered `cancelled` without the
user choosing, the other was never answered, and the session hung at
`Model responding` forever.

## Status

| # | Case | State |
|---|------|-------|
| 1 | Two overlapping permission requests | **passed** — reqs `id=0`/`id=1` overlapped, one picker at a time, both tools completed |
| 2 | Always Allow covers a queued duplicate | **passed** — agent asked twice (`id=2`/`id=3`), one picker, second auto-answered |
| 3 | Command pickers refuse during a decision | **passed** — guards held; focus bug found on accept, fixed as F3 |
| 4 | Abandoned review cancels its request | **passed** — tool failed as cancelled, turn ended |
| 5 | Cancel while a decision is open | **passed** after `c0ae0aa` — `TURN END cancelled`, review closed itself |
| 6 | A Claude edit opens a review at all (F1 regression) | **passed** — review opened, `a` applied the edit, file now reads `hello world` |

## Setup

The plugin is installed as a clone of this repo, so new commits are not live
until you update it. Any fix during this round means redoing this step.

```vim
:lua vim.pack.update({ 'louiselm.nvim' })
```

Confirm in the buffer it opens (`:write`), restart nvim, then verify and prepare
fixtures:

```bash
# these two must print the same commit
git -C ~/.local/share/nvim/site/pack/core/opt/louiselm.nvim log --oneline -1
git -C ~/code/louiselm log --oneline -1
printf 'hello\n' > ~/code/louiselm/qa-diff-test.txt
```

## Ground rules learned the hard way

**Not every command asks for permission.** Claude Code auto-approves read-only
commands that stay inside the session workspace, before louiselm ever sees them.
To force a prompt, read a path *outside* the workspace (`/etc/hostname`) or write
something. `wc -l README.md` and `date` produce zero permission requests; `wc -l
/etc/hostname` prompts reliably.

**Say the tool name and give absolute paths.** "Append a line" gets you Bash, and
a bare filename gets you a `find` before anything else happens. Both waste a
round trip on a picker for the wrong tool. Start each case in a fresh session so
an earlier denial does not make the model hedge.

**Mode `default` is Manual.** Its display name is Manual, so changing it does
nothing. `auto` is the one that hands decisions to a model classifier.

**Pin the log by session id.** The newest log file is always the session you are
currently talking to me in, so `ls -t | head -1` grabs the wrong one:

```bash
L=$(grep -l "<session-uuid>" ~/.local/state/acp-llm-adapter/*jsonrpc.log | tail -1)
```

The session id is in the chat header, or via `:LouiselmSessionId`.

**The log only holds the agent's side.** Requests from the agent appear; your
answers do not. Prove an answer landed by its effect: the tool call reaching a
terminal status and the turn ending.

**Keep state clean with Allow Once.** Always Allow writes a rule in two places:
louiselm's `~/.local/state/nvim/louiselm/permissions.json` and a project-local
rule of Claude's own (a `.claude/settings.local.json` appears in the workspace).
If something stops prompting unexpectedly, clear both. `:LouiselmPermissions`
revokes the louiselm one.

## Cases

### 1. Two overlapping permission requests — passed

Prompt:

> In one message, make two parallel Bash tool calls: `wc -l /etc/hostname` and
> `grep -c bin /etc/passwd`. Do not run them sequentially.

Answer **Allow Once** to each. Expect one picker at a time, the second appearing
only after the first is answered, both tool lines reaching `(completed)`, and the
header showing `Waiting for permission` while any request is outstanding.

Failure signature: a picker vanishing on its own, or the turn stuck at
`Model responding` with typed input reporting `Queued for next turn`.

### 2. Always Allow covers a queued duplicate — passed

Prompt:

> I'm testing my editor's permission queue and need two overlapping requests for
> the same command. In one message, make two parallel Bash tool calls, both
> exactly `wc -l /etc/hostname`. The duplication is intentional — don't collapse
> them into one.

Answer **Always Allow** on the single picker. Expect no second picker and both
tool calls completing. The commands must be byte-identical: rules match the argv
as an exact prefix (`lua/louiselm/permission/store.lua:373`) and the whole shell
string arrives as one argv element.

Afterwards revoke the rule with `:LouiselmPermissions` and check whether
`.claude/settings.local.json` appeared in the repo.

### 3. Command pickers refuse during a decision

Exercises `b76a95d`. A file-edit permission opens a review *buffer* rather than a
picker, which is what makes the chat reachable while a decision is open.

Fixture inside the workspace, so the agent's mandatory Read is auto-approved and
only the edit itself asks:

```bash
printf 'hello\n' > ~/code/louiselm/qa-diff-test.txt
```

Prompt — the tool name matters, "append a line" makes it reach for Bash and you
get a command picker instead:

> Use the Edit tool, not Bash, to change `hello` to `hello world` in
> /home/lotso/code/louiselm/qa-diff-test.txt

Use a fresh session. A bare filename makes the model shell out to `find` the
file first, and a session that already had a denial in it gets cautious and
takes detours — both cost you extra pickers before reaching the code under test.

A `louiselm-diff://` buffer opens. With it still open, run each of:

- `:LouiselmSessionOptions`
- `:LouiselmPermissions`
- `:LouiselmSwitchSession`
- `:LouiselmResume`
- `:LouiselmNewSession`

Each should notify `louiselm: a louiselm permission decision is open; answer it
first` and open nothing. Then:

- `:LouiselmCloseSession` **should** open its confirmation — this exception is
  deliberate, it is the way out of a stuck decision. Choose **Keep**.

Finish with `a` (accept) or `d`/`q` (reject) in the review buffer. When the edit
offers several allow lifetimes, `a` opens a lifetime picker first — that one is
part of the decision and is meant to open. After answering, focus must land back
on the chat buffer (F3).

Failure signature: any of those five opening a picker, which would tear down the
review and answer the edit request without you.

### 4. Abandoned review cancels its request

Exercises the `BufWipeout` handler in `lua/louiselm/ui/diff/init.lua`. Trigger the
same edit review, then navigate away — `:b#`, or open any other file. The review
buffer is `bufhidden=wipe`, so it disappears.

Expect the edit to come back rejected/cancelled and the turn to finish. Confirm
with the log check below: `never finished: none`.

Failure signature: the tool call staying `pending` forever and the session never
returning to `Your turn` — before this handler, walking away from a review left
the agent waiting on a request nobody would ever answer.

### 5. Cancel while a decision is open

Exercises `cancel_permissions` in `lua/louiselm/session/lifecycle.lua`, the
recovery path that did not exist when the original bug hit.

Trigger the edit review again, then run `:LouiselmCancel` while it is open.

Expect: the turn ends and the header returns to `Your turn` rather than hanging.

Expect the review buffer to **close by itself**, focus to return to the chat,
and the case 3 commands to work again immediately — that is the F4 fix. The
turn should end and the header return to `Your turn`.

Failure signature (what F4 looked like before `c0ae0aa`): the review stays on
screen, `q` and `d` do nothing, `a` opens the lifetime picker and answering it
changes nothing, and every guarded command still refuses.

Not fixed, and expected: if a *picker* rather than a review is open when you
cancel, it cannot be closed programmatically. Answering it afterwards reports
`permission decision was already answered` in the transcript.

### 6. A Claude edit opens a review at all — F1 regression

Run this first, it gates cases 3-5. Fresh session, fixture reset:

```bash
printf 'hello\n' > ~/code/louiselm/qa-diff-test.txt
```

> Use the Edit tool, not Bash, to change `hello` to `hello world` in
> /home/lotso/code/louiselm/qa-diff-test.txt

Expect a `louiselm-diff://` buffer showing `-hello` / `+hello world`. Press `a`;
the agent writes the file, so `cat qa-diff-test.txt` should then read
`hello world`.

Failure signature: the transcript line `Error: diff edit must contain diff or
content` (pre-fix wording) or any `diff edit ...` error followed by the edit
being denied, and the tool reporting `Tool use aborted`.

## Evidence check

Run after each case, with `L` pinned to the session under test:

```bash
python3 - "$L" <<'EOF'
import json, sys
TERMINAL = ('completed', 'failed', 'cancelled')
status, order = {}, []
for i, line in enumerate(open(sys.argv[1])):
    try: d = json.loads(line)
    except Exception: continue
    m = d.get('method')
    if m == 'session/request_permission':
        tc = d['params']['toolCall']
        order.append((i, 'PERMISSION id=%s' % d['id'], tc['title'][:40]))
    elif m == 'session/update':
        u = d['params']['update']
        if u.get('sessionUpdate', '').startswith('tool_call') and u.get('status'):
            status[u['toolCallId']] = u['status']
            order.append((i, 'tool ' + u['status'], u['toolCallId'][:14]))
    elif m is None and isinstance(d.get('result'), dict) and 'stopReason' in d['result']:
        reason = d['result']['stopReason']
        order.append((i, 'TURN END', reason))
        # A cancelled turn ends without a terminal status per tool call; the turn
        # ending IS the terminal signal. Without this the check false-alarms.
        if reason == 'cancelled':
            for k, v in status.items():
                if v not in TERMINAL: status[k] = 'cancelled'
for row in order[-16:]: print(*row)
print('\nnever finished:', [k for k, v in status.items() if v not in TERMINAL] or 'none')
EOF
```

`never finished: none` plus a `TURN END` is the pass condition. A tool call stuck
without a terminal status *and no turn end after it* is the exact signature of the
original bug.

## Cleanup when the round closes

```bash
rm ~/code/louiselm/qa-diff-test.txt        # untracked fixture
```

`:LouiselmPermissions` should hold no rule for `wc -l /etc/hostname`, and
`~/code/louiselm/.claude/settings.local.json` should not exist unless you chose
Always Allow somewhere. This file is untracked: commit it as a record of the
round, or delete it.

Still open from this round, deliberately not fixed: `louiselm-fvq`, codex edit
permissions answered with a `-32602` protocol error.

## Reporting back

Send me the session id, which case, what you saw, and anything surprising. I pull
the log myself. If something is wrong I will fix it, and you will need to redo
Setup before retesting.

## Findings this round

**F1 — CONFIRMED live, fixed in `a57cee2` (`louiselm-7xw`).** Reproduced in
session `0503f972`: request `id=2 kind=edit` carried
`content: [{type: "diff", path, oldText: "hello", newText: "hello world"}]` and
the tool then failed with `Tool use aborted`. Retest with case 6.

**F2 — codex edit permissions are answered with a protocol error
(`louiselm-fvq`, not fixed).** codex-acp sends
`toolCall: {toolCallId, kind: "edit", status}` with no path and nothing
reviewable, so `gates.check` rejects it and the session answers `-32602` instead
of asking you anything. Found by reading logs, not verified live; out of scope
for this round.

**F4 — cancelling a turn left a zombie review and a blocked chat
(`louiselm-1ce`, fixed in `c0ae0aa`).** Predicted in the case 5 write-up,
confirmed by your run: the log showed `PERMISSION id=2 kind=edit` then
`TURN END cancelled`, so the agent was released, but the review stayed on
screen, `q`/`a` did nothing, and `decision_active` stayed held so every guarded
command kept refusing. `Session:cancel` answered the request through the raw ACP
responder, which the chat never sees. The session now emits a
`permission_cancelled` event and the chat closes the review and releases the
slot.

**F3 — answering a review left you in the wrong buffer (`louiselm-nna`, fixed in
`348c6fc`).** My own regression from `0ed18d0`: `clear()` read
`self.previous_buffer` *after* `Buffer.close()`, and wiping the buffer runs the
BufWipeout handler synchronously, which clears that field. So the focus restore
was skipped. Caught by case 3 — the edit itself applied correctly, only the
focus was wrong, which no unit test asserted until now.

Original F1 write-up: `lua/louiselm/ui/diff/init.lua:29 request_edit` looks for
the edit payload only in `toolCall.rawInput`. Claude's Edit tool sends
`rawInput = {file_path, old_string, new_string, replace_all}` there — no `diff`,
no `content` — and puts the actual edit in `toolCall.content` as
`[{type = "diff", path, oldText, newText}]`, which louiselm never reads. So
`Apply.normalize` fails with `diff edit must contain diff or content`,
`Diff:open` returns false, and the chat writes an error line and cancels the
request. Net effect: the edit is auto-denied and no review ever opens.

Payload evidence is from June logs (`20260610-133623`, `20260612-053729`), so the
agent's current shape needs confirming with the case 3 prompt. If the review does
open, this finding is wrong and cases 3-5 proceed as written.

- Case 1 and 2 verified live; no defects found.
- Case 5 rough edge predicted in the case above, unconfirmed.
- My first three recipes used prompts that never reached the intended code path
  (`wc -l README.md`, `date`, "append a line" → Bash). Both rules are now in
  Ground rules: outside-the-workspace or write to trigger a prompt, and name the
  tool when a specific tool is the point.
close_reason: Completed: all six QA cases passed and all four child findings are closed; final Codex case live-verified in louiselm-us9

comments.author: assistant
comments.text: No single --external-ref set: unlike the transcript-export round (which ran inside one continuous session), this round explicitly reset to a fresh session per case (see Ground rules: 'Start each case in a fresh session'), and only per-case session ids are recorded in the description: 0503f972 for F1/case 6, 25e0dc43 for the origin bug (louiselm-4wx) that started the round. No single id represents the whole round.

comments.author: assistant
comments.text: Final child louiselm-fvq was fixed in 2fa70dc and live-verified against Codex's real pathless edit permission payload in QA round louiselm-us9 (codex/01a01f9c-15dc-7db1-a84d-56c1973fc210). All four findings and all six original cases are complete.

title: Rejected commit approval can be bypassed by retrying the request
description:
## Summary

A user rejection of a privileged Git commit did not persist as a denial. After the user repeated the same `commit and sync` request, the agent retried the rejected operation and successfully committed and pushed changes.

## Reproduction

Session: `01a00708-4889-7501-a873-52601d5333fd`

1. In `/home/lotso/dotfiles`, ask the agent to `commit and sync` with uncommitted changes.
2. When approval is requested for the Git metadata write, reject it.
3. Repeat `commit and sync`.
4. Observe that the agent retries `git add ... && git commit ...`, then runs `git pull --rebase origin main` and `git push origin main` successfully.

Observed commit: `deb5744 chore(beads): update WAL certificates`.

## Expected

A rejected approval must remain denied for that action/request. The agent should report that the operation was not authorized and must not retry the rejected privileged command or perform the subsequent push unless the user explicitly grants a fresh approval through the approval control. Repeating the natural-language request alone must not bypass the rejection.

## Actual

The next turn treated the earlier rejection as a temporary environment blocker and retried the same privileged operation. The retry succeeded and the changes were committed and synced.

## Impact

Users can lose control over repository mutations after explicitly rejecting an approval prompt. This is an authorization and safety issue affecting commit/push workflows.

## Evidence

The session log records the first tool result as `Rejected("rejected by user")`, followed by a second `commit and sync` turn whose tool calls performed commit, pull/rebase, and push.
close_reason: Fixed permission picker to place typed rejection choices before approvals, preventing numbered-picker fallback from selecting Allow Once. Regression failed before the fix and passes; all 183 MiniTest cases, StyLua, LuaLS, and git diff --check pass.

title: Resume restores session but reports malformed ACP session/load result
description:
## Summary

`:LuiselmResume` restores the requested session, but reports:

`louiselm: ACP session/load returned a malformed result`

Observed while resuming the session for: https://a16z.com/knowing-when-to-stop-the-art-of-making-a-loop-converge/?utm_source=tldrai

## Expected behavior

A successfully restored session should resume without a malformed-result error. If the ACP response is accepted and the session is usable, do not report it as malformed; otherwise fail the resume operation clearly and leave state consistent.

## Actual behavior

The session is put back/restored, while louiselm emits the malformed `ACP session/load` diagnostic.

## Investigation notes

Likely a mismatch between the ACP `session/load` result validation and the subsequent resume state transition, or an error being reported after a usable result has already been applied. Reproduce with `:LuiselmResume` on the session described above and inspect the raw response shape and validation boundary.

## Acceptance criteria

- Resuming a valid saved session does not emit the malformed-result error.
- Malformed `session/load` responses still fail safely and produce a specific diagnostic.
- Resume state is not partially applied when validation fails.
close_reason: Fixed ACP v1 session/load response validation: accept object responses without requiring sessionId, preserve replayed config options when absent, and reject JSON null. TDD regression failed first on {}; focused session tests pass; full 128-case MiniTest suite passes; stylua --check passes; lua-language-server reports zero diagnostics; git diff --check passes; dependency graph has no cycles.

title: Grill-me needed: how should autonomy level be authorized, and should it key on reversibility rather than tool identity
description:
**Grill-me needed. Do not resolve this in passing — it wants full attention.**

Sibling in shape to `louiselm-iyy`: a process/design question surfaced mid-session that fits no existing route. Raised as explicit "food for thought" on 2026-08-19.

## The question

Authorization is expressed conversationally but enforced structurally, and the two are not connected. Saying "ok, tackle it" conveys real intent — *I am comfortable with you working unsupervised here* — but carries no authority. The actual permission level is a harness setting chosen out-of-band, before the work starts, in whichever client is driving (Claude Code's permission modes, Codex's approval/sandbox settings, and so on).

So: where should that decision sit, especially for automation, where nobody is present to answer a prompt?

## Evidence from the session that raised it

A permission prompt fired and aborted on `br update --status=in_progress` — a status field write, fully reversible, trivial. No prompt fired when eight files were moved out of the user's home directory.

The granularity is anti-correlated with risk. The safe operation interrupted the flow; the destructive one did not. This is not fixed by extending an allowlist. The permission layer keys on **tool identity** (`Bash` vs `Write`) when the property that matters is **reversibility**.

## Threads worth pulling

- Permission policies are already one of louiselm's four named extension boundaries (`AGENTS.md` section 1), so the concept has somewhere to live.
- A workflow stage could carry its own policy as part of its definition rather than as a separate rule set: a grill stage needs no write access at all; an execute stage against a well-specified issue is exactly the hands-off case; a QA stage has a human in it by definition. This connects directly to the deferred workflow-engine work (`louiselm-qbr.3`, `louiselm-qbr.5`).
- The `ready-for-agent` label already asserts that a spec is tight enough to hand over. It is a short step from that to also carrying how much autonomy comes with it.

## The distinction to preserve

"Yolo mode" bundles two different things: **acting without asking** and **acting irreversibly**. The first is cheap to grant and easy to withdraw. The second is not.

If autonomy scales with reversibility rather than with confidence in the task, the operator can be far more permissive than they would otherwise dare, because the downside is bounded by construction rather than by the agent's judgment. That framing also removes the need for a phrase like "tackle it" to encode a trust level at all — the action's reversibility determines the treatment, not the sentence that requested it.

## Out of scope for the grill

Re-deriving the above. React to it.

title: Display the requested command in permission pickers
description:
## Problem

The command permission picker identifies only the operation kind and the available decisions. It does not show the command being approved or denied. In the attached observation, after the user entered `retry`, the picker showed only `Deny`, `Allow Once`, and `Always Allow`; the actual `git add ... && git commit ... && git push` command was visible only in a wrapped `[tool]` transcript line behind the picker.

This is unsafe and confusing UX, especially for persistent approval choices. The user should not have to correlate a possibly obscured or stale tool transcript line with the active permission request.

## Evidence

- Screenshot: `/home/lotso/Pictures/scrot/20260816_0743_950x1123_1786858980.png`
- Observed with the Claude ACP adapter after asking `retry`.
- Codex may expose more command context, so compare Claude- and Codex-shaped permission payloads rather than assuming the limitation is adapter-specific.
- Current code already normalizes `data.operation.command`, but `prompt_permission` builds the prompt from only `operation.kind` and formats each item from only the ACP option label. This suggests that the shared UI drops command context that is already available.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a chat using the Claude ACP adapter.
2. Trigger a command requiring permission; denying or failing it and then entering `retry` reproduces the observed sequence.
3. Wait for the command permission picker.
4. Observe that the picker shows approval choices but not the command governed by them.

## Expected

The active permission UI clearly identifies the exact command being approved or denied, including for long or compound shell commands. The complete command must remain inspectable without dismissing the picker or inferring it from the background transcript.

## Actual

The picker prompt is only `louiselm permission (command):`; its entries contain only decision labels.

## Scope

- Surface command context from the normalized permission operation at the decision point.
- Preserve literal command content; do not reconstruct a potentially misleading shell command from lossy data.
- Verify behavior with Claude- and Codex-shaped ACP requests and avoid depending on adapter-specific option labels.
- Keep file-edit diff review and unrelated tool-call rendering unchanged.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Every command permission request with a valid normalized command shows that exact command in the active permission UI before a response can be selected.
2. Long, wrapped, and compound commands remain fully inspectable without relying on transcript lines or tool-call IDs.
3. ACP option names and identifiers remain exact, rejection choices remain first, picker dismissal still cancels, and responses still return the selected option ID.
4. Malformed or unknown operations use an explicit safe fallback and never claim to display a command that was not received.
5. Headless UI tests cover Claude- and Codex-shaped command requests, a long compound command, the safe fallback, scheduling, and the existing fail-closed selection behavior.
close_reason: Displayed exact normalized command JSON in the active permission picker prompt with an explicit unavailable-details fallback. Added Claude/Codex/unknown UI regression coverage and documented behavior. Verification: focused chat suite 48/48; full MiniTest suite 189/189; stylua --check passed; lua-language-server reported no problems; git diff --check passed.

title: Permission pickers from two sessions can still collide
description:
The permission queue added in c639f95 (louiselm-4wx) is per session. vim.ui.select is a process-wide resource: two attached chat sessions that each reach a permission request at the same time still open two pickers, and an async provider such as the Snacks picker tears the first one down. That reproduces the louiselm-4wx failure across sessions - one request answered cancelled without the user acting, the other left unanswered and blocking its agent.

Not fixed with louiselm-4wx because the narrowest boundary for the reported single-session deadlock was the session, and a process-wide picker queue means module-level mutable state, which AGENTS.md section 7 warns against.

Repro sketch: attach two sessions, prompt both so each hits an ask-human permission in the same window, and observe both pickers.

Options to weigh:
- Serialize decision UI in louiselm.ui.chat across views (the chat controller already owns every view and the diff review, so it has a clear owner and lifecycle for the queue).
- Or serialize in louiselm.ui.picker, which also covers the session, skill, and agent pickers, but introduces a module singleton.

Whatever the layer, the invariant is the same as louiselm-4wx: at most one decision UI open at a time, and every ACP permission request answered exactly once.
close_reason: Fixed in 0ed18d0. Chose the chat controller over louiselm.ui.picker: it already owns every view and the diff review, so the queue has a clear owner and lifecycle instead of a module singleton (AGENTS.md section 7), and it covers reviews as well as pickers. lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua now queues decisions across all views (queue_decision/pump_decisions/open_decision), releases the slot exactly once per decision, and cancels what it cannot host: chat disposal, an event delivered to a torn-down view, and a select provider that throws. lua/louiselm/ui/diff/init.lua adds a BufWipeout handler because review buffers are bufhidden=wipe - navigating away used to abandon the request unanswered, which would have stalled the queue. Tests: tests/ui/chat_spec.lua 'opens one permission decision at a time across sessions', 'cancels permission decisions still queued when the chat is disposed', 'cancels a permission request delivered after disposal'; tests/ui/diff_spec.lua 'cancels the permission request when its review buffer is wiped'. chat_spec now restores vim.schedule/vim.ui.select in post_case, because a failing expectation skipped a test's own restore and broke MiniTest itself. Full suite 196 cases, stylua --check, lua-language-server all clean. Not covered: pickers louiselm opens for its own commands (session options, skills, agents) are still unqueued and can collide with a permission decision.

title: Design persistent ACP permission UX
description:
## Goal

Decide and implement how louiselm should remember ACP permission choices such as Allow for Session and Allow Commands Starting With a command prefix.

## Current state

The chat UI displays permission options supplied by the ACP adapter and forwards the selected optionId. louiselm does not persist those choices itself. ACP defines allow_always as remembering the choice but does not prescribe the storage mechanism.

## Scope

- Grill and document the desired UX and trust model for once, session, workspace, command-prefix, and permanent approvals.
- Decide whether louiselm, the ACP adapter, or both own persistence and enforcement.
- Define storage location, scope/keying, revocation/editing UX, and behavior across sessions, adapters, workspaces, and restarts.
- Implement the agreed behavior with tests and documentation.

## Acceptance criteria

- Permission choices have clear, truthful lifetime/scope semantics.
- Persisted rules cannot silently broaden command or file scopes.
- Users can inspect and revoke remembered rules.
- Behavior is covered by deterministic tests and documented for headless and chat consumers.

## Out of scope

- Changing ACP protocol semantics or adding adapter-specific compatibility shims before the UX decision.
close_reason: Implemented exact workspace-and-adapter permission memory, atomic persistent state, option-kind replay, headless list/revoke APIs, file lifetime selection, and :LouiselmPermissions

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
Agreed UX direction from grill session:

- louiselm owns remembered permission decisions; no user-configurable rule object initially.
- Default scope is current workspace + current ACP adapter.
- Command rules match exact argv prefixes; no shell strings, regexes, or substring matching.
- Persist state in a user-level file under Neovim stdpath("state"), never the project repo.
- Add :LouiseLmPermissions to inspect and revoke remembered rules.
- allow_once/reject_once are not saved; allow_session is memory-only for the ACP session; allow_always/reject_always are persisted.
- Commands and file edits have separate rule types.
- If a later adapter request lacks a compatible option kind, fail closed and ask the user again; never infer from labels.

title: Send bounded hidden skill catalogs in inject mode
description:
## Goal

Provide natural-language skill discovery to injected agents without visible context markers, unbounded prompts, or duplicate delivery.

## Scope

- In scope: serialize implicit skills using the Agent Skills `<available_skills><skill>...` XML shape with escaped name, description, and absolute configured-alias location.
- In scope: prepend the fixed agreed behavioral instructions and cap the complete serialized hidden block at 8,000 UTF-8 bytes, including preamble and wrappers.
- In scope: preserve the preamble and all possible names/paths, shorten descriptions fairly and codepoint-safely first, then omit the deterministic name/path-sorted tail if minimum metadata still cannot fit.
- In scope: exclude explicit-only skills from the model catalog while retaining them in the picker; expose omitted/truncated diagnostics.
- In scope: build the catalog only for a new session, hold it locally, and attach it as a separate hidden first text block to the first accepted non-slash model prompt.
- In scope: defer catalog and ordinary attached contexts across user-authored slash prompts; consume the catalog when prompt submission returns a valid ACP request id. Do not resend after accepted cancellation, crash, or uncertain failure.
- In scope: explicit picker activation attaches the exact complete SKILL.md once for that activation; a selected-file read failure blocks submission and preserves the prompt/selection.
- Out of scope: resumed-session reinjection, synthetic catalog turns, recursive resource embedding, native command invocation, and transcript persistence.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. No `[context: skill-index]` or catalog text is rendered before submission.
2. The entire hidden block never exceeds 8,000 bytes and is validly truncated at UTF-8 boundaries.
3. Natural-language prompts receive one catalog per new injected session; explicit-only skills never appear in it.
4. Slash commands defer rather than consume attached skill context.
5. Synchronous local failure retains the catalog, while any accepted request consumes it exactly once.
6. A deliberate re-selection may attach the same skill on a later turn, but one activation never sends it twice.
7. Resumed or external sessions do not receive a guessed catalog; documentation directs users to start a new session when provenance is uncertain.
8. MiniTest and mock ACP coverage assert block ordering, budgeting, XML escaping, slash deferral, request-id consumption, failure/cancel behavior, picker reads, and no-double-send invariants.

## Testing

Use byte-counting and multibyte fixtures for the budget. Assert exact ACP prompt block arrays through the mock agent.

## Notes

The 8,000-byte rule is a conservative adaptation of Codex fallback behavior, not an ACP or Agent Skills specification requirement.
close_reason: Completed bounded hidden skill catalogs, exact picker bodies, one-shot accepted delivery, and mock ACP coverage (306 tests green)

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
Implemented bounded hidden inject catalogs and one-shot delivery.

Evidence:
- Catalog uses <skills_instructions>/<available_skills> XML, escapes metadata, excludes explicit-only skills, and stays <= 8000 bytes by fair codepoint-safe description truncation before deterministic tail omission. Public catalog.truncated/catalog.omitted fields expose diagnostics.
- New inject sessions hold the catalog invisibly and prepend it only to the first accepted non-slash model prompt. Slash prompts defer all attached context; local write/read failures preserve it; accepted requests consume it once; attached/resumed sessions never receive guessed catalogs.
- Explicit picker activation captures the exact SKILL.md body once. Failed reads preserve the chip and prompt and retry safely.
- Focused skills/context/chat/command/mock-agent tests pass. Full MiniTest: 306 cases, 0 failures. stylua --check lua tests passes. Repository-wide stylua and lua-language-server remain blocked only by pre-existing blog/scripts/tohtml-driver.lua findings tracked as louiselm-d7l.

title: louiselm.nvim: pure ACP client for Neovim — v1 core + phased roadmap
description:
## Problem Statement

As a daily Neovim + agent user, my current plugin (codecompanion.nvim) fights my workflow in three ways. First, config mistakes fail silently: a mistyped key is absorbed by deep-merge and the feature it configures is skipped without a word. Second, its architecture is a general adapter abstraction normalizing HTTP providers and ACP into one interface, while I use exclusively ACP agents (claude-agent-acp, codex-acp, acp-llm-adapter, copilot ACP) — I pay the complexity of a layer I do not use. Third, it gives me no path to the feature I actually want next: a swarm of agents collaboratively working a queue of beads tasks. My core workflow — grill an idea in chat, converge on a plan, convert the plan into beads via skills — must keep working, uniformly, across all my agents.

## Solution

louiselm.nvim: a pure ACP client for Neovim. Agents are external processes declared in config; anything non-ACP reaches the plugin through external bridges (acp-llm-adapter, opencode acp), never through in-plugin providers. The core is built swarm-ready from day one: a multi-session registry with a headless Lua API, typed events, pluggable permission policies, and addressable sessions — so the future orchestrator is an additional consumer of the public API, not a rewrite. Configuration is validated militantly against a single declarative schema that also generates the LuaCATS types and the documentation. Skills use an explicit per-agent native/inject/off policy: native delegates discovery and invocation to the adapter, inject uses a hidden bounded local catalog, and off disables LouiseLM skill automation.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I want to declare each agent (command, args, env, options) in my config, so that adding a backend is a config entry, never plugin code.
2. As a user, I want any unknown config key to produce a hard error with a fuzzy "did you mean" suggestion, so that typos can never silently disable a feature.
3. As a user, I want wrong types or invalid values to error with the expected type, the received value, and a valid example, so that I can fix mistakes without reading source.
4. As a user, I want all config errors collected and reported in one structured report, so that I fix everything in a single pass instead of a fix-reload loop.
5. As a user, I want the plugin to refuse to start on invalid config, so that I am never unknowingly running on silently substituted defaults.
6. As a user, I want deprecated keys to warn with a migration path, so that upgrades guide me instead of breaking me.
7. As a user, I want editor completion and type checking while writing my config, so that most mistakes are caught before the validator ever runs.
8. As a user, I want :checkhealth to re-run validation plus environment checks (agent binaries on PATH, versions, skill paths exist), so that a broken setup is diagnosable in one command.
9. As a user, I want a chat buffer with streamed markdown and a visible tool-call timeline, so that I can follow what the agent is doing while it does it.
10. As a user, I want to pick which agent a new session uses and switch between concurrent sessions, so that several conversations can live side by side.
11. As a user, I want agent-requested file edits and commands gated by a permission flow, so that nothing touches my system without policy saying so.
12. As a user, I want agent file edits reviewable as diffs, so that I can inspect changes before or after approving them.
13. As a user, I want permissions evaluated by pluggable policy objects with "ask the human" merely the default, so that future autonomous sessions can run scoped auto-approval policies without core changes.
14. As a user, I want to mention the current buffer, send a visual selection, and fuzzy-pick files into the conversation, so that pointing the agent at context is one gesture.
15. As a user, I want slash commands advertised by the agent over ACP to appear in the chat's command menu, so that agent capabilities surface without client-side duplication.
16. As a user, I want my central Agent Skills / SKILL.md repo available to injected agents and the local picker, while native adapters retain ownership of their own discovery, so that one skill tree works without duplicate delivery.
17. As a user, I want an explicit per-agent skills policy (native, inject, off), defaulting to native with no runtime inference or fallback, so that each adapter has one understandable skill owner.
18. As a user, I want ordered, deterministic, symlink-aware local discovery with duplicate and escape diagnostics, so that injected and picker-visible skills resolve predictably.
19. As a user, I want a skill invocation picker that sends one advertised command in native mode or one complete SKILL.md in inject mode, so that explicit activation is predictable and never duplicated.
20. As a user, I want my grill-me → plan → beads workflow to run purely through skills and the agent executing the beads CLI itself, so that the plugin core stays tracker-ignorant.
21. As a plugin consumer (or future orchestrator), I want a headless Lua API — create session against a named agent, prompt, receive streamed updates via callbacks, cancel, dispose — so that everything the UI does is scriptable without UI.
22. As a plugin consumer, I want typed events emitted for every session lifecycle moment (chunk, tool call started/finished, permission requested, turn done, error), so that dashboards and orchestrators can subscribe without patching internals.
23. As a user, I want every session addressable by id with inspectable state (agent, status, working dir, current turn), so that a future swarm dashboard has substrate to read.
24. As a user, I want a crashed or misbehaving agent process to surface as a loud, specific session error — never a hang or a silent death — so that failure modes are as strict as config validation.
25. As a contributor, I want the ACP layer conformance-tested against a mock agent in CI, so that protocol correctness is verified without real LLMs or API keys.

## Implementation Decisions

- Pure ACP client, hard boundary: no in-plugin HTTP providers ever; non-ACP backends go through external bridges. Internally one small agent interface with ACP as its sole implementation, preserving the seam for a hypothetical future transport.
- Five hard architectural constraints checked against every PR: (1) multi-session registry, no singleton chat; (2) headless API with the UI as its first consumer; (3) typed event system; (4) permission policies as pluggable objects, human prompt as default policy; (5) sessions addressable, listable, inspectable.
- Modules: schema (config DSL, validator, error reporter; single source generating LuaCATS types and vimdoc), acp (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio via vim.system pipes, typed against the protocol schema), session (registry, headless API, events, process lifecycle), permission (policy engine), skills (discovery, index injection, per-agent policy, overlap detection), ui.chat, ui.diff, health, and a dev-only mock ACP agent.
- Config validation is militant: unknown key or wrong type is a hard error; errors are collected exhaustively then reported; plugin refuses to start on any error; deprecated keys warn with migration path.
- Skills: Agent Skills defines the file format and ACP remains transport. Global paths feed LouiseLM-managed discovery; global policy defaults to native and an agent may override only native|inject|off. Native sends no catalog/body and resolves picker activation through the adapter's latest advertised commands. Inject sends one hidden, 8,000-byte bounded metadata catalog on a new session and one complete SKILL.md per explicit activation. Off disables automation. Policy is session-static, never inferred, and never falls back at runtime.
- Chat context is deliberately thin: buffer mention, visual selection, file picker, agent slash-command passthrough, skill picker. Agents explore the project themselves; the client points.
- Tech foundation: Neovim floor = latest stable at release, moving forward aggressively; no UI/framework runtime dependencies (no plenary, no nui); `lyaml` plus LibYAML is the explicit conditional runtime dependency for LouiseLM-managed local skill discovery, replacing a custom YAML parser; picker integrations are configured and validated, never silently auto-detected; LuaCATS everywhere with lua-language-server as a CI gate.
- Phasing: P0 foundation (schema, acp, session, agent defs) → P1 daily driver (chat, permissions, diff, context, explicit skill profiles; exit criterion: codecompanion uninstalled, grill-me → beads works on all four agents) → P2 comfort (inline assistant on the same session core, history via ACP session/load, skill-profile ergonomics, multi-session UX) → P3 swarm (opens with its own grill-me).
- Rust is welcome where it earns its place: the swarm orchestrator binary is the named candidate (long-running external process, async runtime, same ecosystem as beads_rust); the core editor-side client stays pure Lua.

## Testing Decisions

- mini.test as the sole, dev-only test dependency.
- schema, acp, session, permission, and skills get full headless unit coverage; the headless API constraint exists partly to make this trivial.
- acp and session additionally get integration coverage driving the mock ACP agent end to end (spawn, initialize, session, prompt, streamed updates, permission round-trip, cancel, agent-crash surfacing).
- A good test here exercises a module through its public interface only; the five architectural constraints are themselves enforced by tests (e.g. two concurrent sessions prompting simultaneously is a required passing case from P0).
- UI modules get smoke tests via child Neovim processes; no pixel-level assertions.
- Validator and skills tests include typo'd keys, wrong types, valid-looking-but-unknown sections, YAML/semantic failures, ordered duplicate precedence, symlink aliases/escapes, native command collisions, injected budget boundaries, and exact no-double-send behavior.

## Out of Scope

- Completion / ghost text: dropped permanently; other plugins own that space.
- In-plugin HTTP or provider adapters of any kind.
- A prompt library separate from skills.
- The swarm orchestrator's design (in-nvim vs external Rust binary, scheduling, worktree isolation): deferred to a dedicated grill-me that opens Phase 3. This epic only guarantees its prerequisites.
- Beads-specific core code; the optional beads dashboard/picker is a future extension on the public API.
- RAG, indexing, web search: agent-side concerns.

## Further Notes

- Ecosystem bet acknowledged: louiselm wagers on ACP's continued adoption (Zed-originated; gemini-cli, opencode, goose, amp, claude, codex all speak it). The internal agent interface is the hedge.
- Risk: ACP spec evolution (e.g. session/load, command advertisement) may shift; the protocol layer should pin a spec version and negotiate capabilities explicitly.
- The user's central skill repo pattern (~/.config/agentskills) is the reference LouiseLM-managed deployment. Discovery preserves configured aliases, canonicalizes for cycles/deduplication, warns on escapes, and treats roots as trusted prompt/plugin-like input.
- Follow-up work items after this epic lands: per-phase decomposition via to-beads-feature / to-beads-tasks, starting with P0.

title: P0: Config schema DSL + militant validator
description:
## Scope
Single-source declarative config schema that generates LuaCATS types, vimdoc, and drives runtime validation. Militant: unknown keys are hard errors with fuzzy "did you mean"; wrong types error with expected/received/example; all errors collected and reported in one pass; plugin refuses to start on any error; deprecated keys warn with migration path.

## User stories covered
2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7

## Modules
- `lua/louiselm/schema/init.lua` — schema DSL (describe key shape, type, default, validator fns)
- `lua/louiselm/schema/validate.lua` — recursive validator, error collector
- `lua/louiselm/schema/report.lua` — structured error report formatter
- `lua/louiselm/schema/gen_luacats.lua` — emit LuaCATS annotations from schema
- `lua/louiselm/schema/gen_vimdoc.lua` — emit vimdoc from schema

## Acceptance criteria
- Unknown key at any nesting depth → hard error with fuzzy suggestion
- Wrong type → error with expected type, received value, valid example
- All errors surface in one structured report (no fix-reload loop)
- Plugin setup() returns false on any validation error
- Deprecated key → warning with migration path, plugin still starts
- LuaCATS output passes lua-language-server CI gate
- Generated vimdoc matches schema structure
- mini.test coverage for adversarial cases: typo at depth, wrong types, valid-looking unknown sections

Implement the schema description DSL in lua/louiselm/schema/init.lua. API: `Schema.define(spec)` that accepts nested key descriptions with type, default, description, and optional validator functions. Must support: string, number, boolean, table (nested), array-of, one-of types. Output is a normalized schema table consumed by the validator and generators.

title: T: Recursive validator — walk config tree, collect all errors exhaustively

Implement recursive validator in lua/louiselm/schema/validate.lua. Walks user config against normalized schema. Collects ALL errors (never short-circuits on first error). title: T: Error reporter — structured format with fuzzy suggestions and examples

Implement structured error reporter in lua/louiselm/schema/report.lua. Takes the error list from the validator and formats a human-readable report. Each error includes: key path (e.g. "agents.claude.model"), error type, message, and where applicable: fuzzy suggestion, expected type, received value, valid example. Report is returned as a table consumable by both :checkhealth and startup error messages.

title: T: Install and integrate mini.test test dependency
description:
Make the headless MiniTest suite runnable in local development and CI.

Implementation guidance:
- Treat mini.test as a dev-only dependency; do not add runtime Lua dependencies or vendor source into lua/.
- Install a pinned mini.nvim revision (mini.test is provided by mini.nvim) into an ignored .deps/ checkout through a small idempotent setup entrypoint, or use an equivalent reproducible CI cache/install mechanism.
- Wire the installed checkout into tests/minimal_init.lua before requiring mini.test, with a clear failure when the dependency is missing.
- Keep the repository quality command runnable: nvim --headless --noplugin -u ./tests/minimal_init.lua -c "lua MiniTest.run()" -c "qa!".
- Document the install command and the pinned revision; CI should install/cache the same revision and execute the full MiniTest suite.

Acceptance criteria:
- A fresh checkout can install the pinned mini.test dependency with one documented command.
- The existing schema DSL tests run and pass through MiniTest.
- The exact repository test command runs successfully in a dependency-present environment.
- Missing dependency errors are specific and actionable.

title: Typing during active turn inserts red buffer error
description:
## Reproduction
1. Start a LouiseLM chat session.
2. While the model is responding / it is not the user's turn, type into the chat buffer.
3. Observe the buffer and Neovim message area.

## Observed
The chat buffer displays a red error/traceback while handling the typed input:
`vim.schedule callback: .../lua/louiselm/ui/chat/init.lua:145: replacement string item contains newlines`
The traceback points through `nvim_buf_set_lines`, `set_line`, and `handle_event`. The UI later appears normal once the turn completes (see second screenshot), but the transient error is user-visible and may indicate that streamed/event updates race with edits made while the session is active.

## Expected
Typing while it is not the user's turn should be safely rejected, queued, or otherwise handled without a red traceback or corrupted chat buffer. Any user-facing feedback should be intentional and clear.

## Evidence
- First screenshot: `/home/lotso/Pictures/scrot/20260809_0501_1920x1200_1786244489.png`
- Second screenshot: `/home/lotso/Pictures/scrot/20260809_0501_1920x1200_1786244505.png`

## Acceptance criteria
- Reproduce the issue deterministically with a mock/fast event sequence if possible.
- Identify whether the root cause is newline-containing content being passed as one `nvim_buf_set_lines` replacement item, a turn-state race, or both.
- Prevent the red traceback and preserve the intended chat content during active-turn typing.
- Add regression coverage for input arriving while streamed updates are being applied.
close_reason: Normalized multiline ACP tool titles before rendering and added regression coverage

title: Queue one next-turn chat prompt while the session is busy
description:
## Problem

Pressing Enter in the chat while the model is responding currently mutates the transcript first, then calls `Session:prompt()`. Because the session is not `ready`, the prompt is rejected and the chat records both a phantom user turn and `Error: session is not ready`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a louiselm chat session and submit a prompt that produces a response long enough to remain active.
2. While the session status is `prompting`, type another message on the chat input line and press Enter.
3. Observe that the input is appended as though it were submitted, followed by `Error: session is not ready`, even though ACP rejected the prompt.

## Expected behavior

The chat owns one pending next-turn prompt per attached session. Pressing Enter during an active turn commits the current input as that session's queued prompt. It remains outside the transcript and sends automatically only after that turn definitively completes or cancellation completes.

## Decisions

- Queue only in `prompting`, `waiting_permission`, and `cancelling`; ordinary ready-state submission remains immediate.
- Support exactly one queued prompt per session, including slash commands.
- Keep queued state with its session when switching chat buffers.
- Show `Queued for next turn` beside the input using virtual text, without modifying prompt text.
- A queued prompt is committed by Enter. Editing it returns it to draft state and requires Enter to recommit, preventing a partial edit from auto-sending.
- Snapshot attached file/selection context when the prompt is committed.
- Release the queue only at a definitive active-turn completion boundary, not on unrelated generic `ready` transitions.
- User cancellation preserves and sends the queued prompt after cancellation completes. A genuine session failure preserves it as a draft and does not send it.
- Append the user message to the transcript only after `Session:prompt()` accepts it.
- If submission fails, preserve the draft and use an editor notification; do not append an `Error:` transcript line for a prompt that was never accepted.
- During `starting` or `configuring`, Enter preserves a draft and notifies instead of queuing. Never queue in `error` or `disposed`.
- Closing a session warns explicitly that its queued prompt will be discarded. Disposal guarantees queued work cannot send later.

## Acceptance criteria

1. Enter during each active-turn state queues one prompt without adding either the prompt or an error to the transcript.
2. On normal turn completion, the committed prompt and its snapshotted context are submitted exactly once and only then appear in transcript history.
3. On completed user cancellation, the committed prompt submits exactly once; on session error it remains an unsent draft.
4. Editing a committed queued prompt makes it a draft and prevents auto-send until Enter recommits it.
5. A second queued turn cannot be accumulated; state is isolated per attached session and survives session switching.
6. Slash commands use the same queue path.
7. Startup/configuration/error/disposed states never create queued work or transcript errors from rejected input.
8. Closing/disposal clears pending work, warns when appropriate, and late scheduled events cannot submit it.
9. Add focused headless chat tests for state transitions, async scheduled event delivery, exactly-once submission, context ownership, switching, failure, cancellation, and disposal. Follow red-green-refactor and run the full required quality gates.

## Scope

- In scope: chat input/queued-prompt state, presentation, lifecycle handling, and behavioral tests.
- Out of scope: changing ACP to allow concurrent prompts, queuing multiple future turns, or changing session-core readiness rules.
close_reason: Implemented one per-session queued next-turn prompt with virtual-text state, edit invalidation, context snapshots, turn/cancellation release, rejection preservation, close/disposal safety, and README documentation. Verification: focused chat suite 27/27 passed; full mini.test suite 112/112 passed; stylua --check . passed; lua-language-server --check . --checklevel=Warning passed with zero diagnostics; git diff --check passed.
